steps.title: Pull request 336, told in pictures and code
steps.text: This version leans on diagrams: each part of the change is drawn first, then shown in code. Scroll, and the panel follows the step in the box: the ticket, a diagram, or the code.

steps.title: Why it changed
steps.text: Your chat app lists a session only when the agent is the pane's own process. A clerk the postmaster opened ran as the child of a helper shell instead, so the app saw the shell and showed a plain terminal. One clerk waited more than a day for an answer.

steps.title: What done looks like
steps.text: The agent takes the shell's place, so the pane's own process is the agent and the app lists the session. Its environment stays the same, and the launches that run without you work as before.

steps.title: Four things had to be true
steps.text: The ticket names four criteria. Each gets its own section below, in order: pictures of the mechanism first, then the code that makes it true and the test that shows it.

find: A booking clerk or a postmaster that the flow opens in a pane
steps.title: The agent is the pane's own process
steps.text: The first criterion is the fix itself. The next pictures show what the app looks at, why the agent failed it, and what changed.

steps.title: What the app looks at
steps.text: A terminal serves one process group at a time, and the app lists a session when that group is the agent's own. Before the change the agent had its own id, but it sat in bash's group, and the terminal served bash.

steps.title: Why: bash forked the agent
steps.text: The helper started the agent the usual way. It forked a child with a new id, waited for it, and exited with its status, so bash stayed in the pane the whole time.

steps.title: The old helper in code
steps.text: Here is that helper. `"$@"` starts the agent as a child, and `s=$?; exit $s` waits for it and passes its status on.

steps.title: Every launch used that helper
steps.text: Every role with an environment file went through it: the sessions opened for you, and the launches that run without you.

steps.title: The fix: exec
steps.text: With `exec`, the shell does not start a child. It replaces itself with the agent, which keeps the shell's id and its hold on the terminal.

steps.title: The new helper in code
steps.text: `sourcedExec` keeps the old helper's start and ends with `exec` instead. It goes through `env`, for a reason the next section shows.

steps.title: Only your sessions switch
steps.text: Only the sessions opened for you use the new helper. The launches that run without you keep the old one, as Decision 1 says, for a reason criterion 3 shows.

steps.title: The one line that switches
steps.text: The interactive form, the command that starts a session in a pane, now calls `sourcedExec` where it called `sourcedLaunch`.

steps.title: Now the numbers match
steps.text: The agent's id, its group and the group the terminal serves are now the same, so the app lists the session.

steps.title: How the tests show it
steps.text: A stand-in named `claude` goes first on the path. The test types the form into an interactive bash on a pseudo-terminal, as a pane does, and the stand-in prints what it sees on a PROBE line.

steps.title: Reading the third number
steps.text: To print the group the terminal serves, the stand-in uses the shared process module, which now reports it as `terminal` for every process.

steps.title: On Linux and on macOS
steps.text: On Linux the number is field 5 of the process's `stat` file. macOS has none, so the module asks `ps` for one more column, `tpgid`, and each later column moves along by one.

steps.title: Typed into a pseudo-terminal
steps.text: `script` gives the test a pseudo-terminal on both Linux and macOS, with different arguments on each, and runs an interactive bash in it.

steps.title: What counts as passing
steps.text: The check passes when the three numbers on the PROBE line match.

steps.title: The cases for criterion 1
steps.text: A clerk and a postmaster on a pseudo-terminal, and a clerk as a tmux window's own command. The Herdr case needs a live pane, so it was checked by hand.

steps.title: The tests in code
steps.text: Each case writes a config whose role has an env file, prints the form for that role and runs the check.

find: The agent in such a session starts with the same environment
A session keeps loading its role's environment file
steps.title: The same environment as before
steps.text: Replacing the shell must not change what the agent starts with, including what the role's env file sets. Decision 2 keeps loading that file.

steps.title: What the helper does, in order
steps.text: Stage 3 loads the role's env file and stage 4 drops the flow's launch names, so the agent starts with what the file sets, such as a provider key, as before.

steps.title: Stages 3 and 4 in code
steps.text: `set -a` exports everything the file sets, and the flow's two internal launch names are removed before the agent starts.

steps.title: Finding env first
steps.text: Stage 2 looks up `env` before the file runs, while the path is still the flow's. A file that changes the path or defines its own `env` cannot take over the launch.

steps.title: Stage 2 in code
steps.text: The path to `env` is kept in a variable that is never exported, and an `exit` in the file still stops the launch before any agent starts.

steps.title: Where the level could go wrong
steps.text: Stage 1 sets the shell level the agent should see, and stage 5 hands it over. A plain `exec` would change it on the way.

steps.title: A plain exec lowers the level
steps.text: Bash lowers the exported `SHLVL` by one when it runs `exec`, so the agent would see 0 where it used to see 1.

steps.title: Through env, it stays
steps.text: Running the agent through `env` with the level set hands back the level the file left. The older bash on macOS behaves the same.

steps.title: Stage 5 in code
steps.text: With a level set, the agent runs through `env "SHLVL=$SHLVL"`; with none, through `env -u SHLVL`, so an unset level stays unset.

steps.title: What counts as passing
steps.text: The agent must see shell level 1, the file's `FOO=bar`, the parent's variables, and neither internal launch name.

steps.title: The cases for criterion 2
steps.text: The same pseudo-terminal runs check the environment, and four kinds of env file are tried.

steps.title: The tests in code
steps.text: A file that sets a variable, one that sets the level to 9, one that exits with status 3 so no agent may start, and a role with no file at all.

find: The launches that run without the user, which are
Only the sessions opened for the user change
steps.title: Launches without you work as before
steps.text: Workhorses, reviewers, coachmen and a headless postmaster must start and end exactly as they did. Decision 1 keeps them on the old helper.

steps.title: Why they keep the fork
steps.text: When an agent is killed, bash sees it and exits with status 143, and the launcher reads that as a normal status. The wall record relies on it.

steps.title: What exec would break
steps.text: With `exec` there is no shell in between. The launcher would see the signal itself, record the agent as stopped and re-raise the signal on itself.

steps.title: The reason, in the code
steps.text: The comment above the new helper says why the background launches stay on `sourcedLaunch`.

steps.title: A stand-in that kills itself
steps.text: The test starts a real background coachman launch with an env file. Its stand-in agent sends itself the terminate signal straight away.

steps.title: Reported, and survived
steps.text: The launcher has to exit with status 143 and not be killed by the signal. Both `muse` and `claude` are tried, because an `exec` in the shared helper breaks this for `muse`.

find: A fixture run from this branch scores clean.
steps.title: A fixture run scores clean
steps.text: This criterion is shown by a run, not by code.

steps.title: Why a fixture run was needed
steps.text: The launcher is part of the coachman's contract, so the change could merge only after a full test run of the flow from its branch scored clean.

steps.title: 11 of 11
steps.text: The pull request reports the fixture run clean, 11 of 11 checks, at its final commit, with the gate passing there and no serious review finding open.
